Many poems, sayings and proverbs are collected in this section of the book of Proverbs. Some were written or collected by people who are named. This includes Solomon, Hezekiah and Agur. Others were written or collected by people who aren’t named. This includes the sayings of a group called the wise people (Proverbs 22:17 – 24:34).

People can become wise when God gives them wisdom. This was true in Solomon’s case. The story about this is recorded in 1 Kings 3:1–15. People can also become wise by studying the world around them. This includes studying plants, animals, weather, other people and everything God made. As people study, they gain knowledge. They come to understand many things about how life works. These are lessons or patterns that they have noticed. When knowledge and understanding are combined with respect for God, they become godly wisdom.

For hundreds of years in Israel, wise people shared with others these lessons and patterns. They shared them through poems, sayings and proverbs. The poems, sayings and proverbs in this section give instruction about many different matters. These matters include anger, jealousy, arguing, food, honour, being humble and pride. They include relationships in family groups, between husbands and wives and between parents and children. They include relationships in communities, between men and women and between friends and neighbours. They include money and relationships between rich people and poor people. They include matters of work, being lazy, farming, business and trade. They include justice and matters of courts and of government. They also include the mind, heart, mouth and ears of each person. All the instructions teach about doing what is right and fair.
A king was the most powerful person in an ancient nation, and it seemed he could do anything he wanted. However, God guides the king's heart.
This proverb is almost exactly the same in {{Proverbs 16:2|Proverbs 16:2}}.
God wants worship to come from a sincere heart and lead to good actions (see {{Psalm 40:6-8|Psalm 40:6–8}}; {{Micah 6:6-8|Micah 6:6–8}}).

Appearance (eyes), character (heart), and actions are all important. God dislikes pride (see {{Proverbs 6:17-18|Proverbs 6:17–18}}; {{Proverbs 11:2|11:2}}; {{Proverbs 13:10|13:10}}; {{Proverbs 15:33|15:33}}; {{Proverbs 16:18|16:18}}; {{Proverbs 18:12|18:12}}).
The path of foolishness leads to death, while the road of wisdom leads to life.

A marriage that appears good from the outside, like in a beautiful home, is not fulfilling if it is full of arguments (see also {{Proverbs 21:19|Proverbs 21:19}}; {{Proverbs 25:24|25:24}}; {{Proverbs 27:15-17|27:15–17}}; compare {{Proverbs 11:22|11:22}}; {{Proverbs 12:4|12:4b}}). See the parallel passage in {{Proverbs 25:24|Proverbs 25:24}}
Evil people do not just do bad things; they are bad. No argument will change their behavior.
The simple-minded learn when they see a mocker punished (see {{Proverbs 1:22|Proverbs 1:22}}; {{Proverbs 19:25|19:25}}). The wise do not need punishment threats because they already seek wisdom.
*The Righteous One*: God observes the wicked actions done in private and will punish them for their sins. Alternatively, *the Righteous One* could mean the wisdom of any righteous person.
God is fair, so he rewards good people and punishes bad ones. This is why good people love justice, and bad people fear it.
People with common sense can avoid life's dangers.
Spending on wine and luxury stops people from saving money. They choose to spend instead of save.
The wicked will get caught in the traps they set for others ({{Proverbs 26:27|Proverbs 26:27}}; see also {{Proverbs 11:8|11:8}}).
*Better to live in the desert*: Compare {{Proverbs 21:9|Proverbs 21:9}}; {{Proverbs 25:24|25:24}}.

Righteousness and unfailing love are traits linked to Israel's agreement with God (see {{Exodus 34:5-7|Exodus 34:5–7}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:9-11|Deuteronomy 7:9–11}}). The agreement promised life and honor to those who followed God's law ({{Deuteronomy 28:1-14|Deuteronomy 28:1–14}}).

A smart military planner can find ways to beat stronger armies. This shows that wisdom is better than just strength (compare {{Ecclesiastes 7:12|Ecclesiastes 7:12}}; {{Ecclesiastes 9:13-18|9:13–18}}).
*Mocker*: See {{Proverbs 1:25-27|Proverbs 1:25–27}} and {{Proverbs 9:7-9|9:7–9}}. Also, see study note on Proverbs 1:22.

Generosity is a trait of the godly, while stinginess is a trait of fools ({{Proverbs 29:7|Proverbs 29:7}}, {{Proverbs 29:14|14}}). Interestingly, the more you give, the more you receive ({{Proverbs 11:24|Proverbs 11:24}}).

Human wisdom is powerless against the Lord (see {{Proverbs 16:1|Proverbs 16:1}}, {{Proverbs 16:3|3}}, {{Proverbs 16:9|9}}, {{Proverbs 16:33|33}}). Similarly, military power, symbolized by the horse, is powerless without the Lord's blessing.
A wise person will not risk their reputation for money.
Remembering that the Lord created both rich and poor helps stop the exploitation of the poor.

The idea of being careful appears in several proverbs ({{Proverbs 14:8|Proverbs 14:8}}, {{Proverbs 14:15|15}}; {{Proverbs 21:29|21:29}}). See the parallel passage in {{Proverbs 27:12|Proverbs 27:12.}}

*Fear of the LORD* (see {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}; {{Proverbs 9:10|9:10}}) is closely linked with humility. A humble person understands he is not the center of the universe. Humility is more valuable than wealth ({{Proverbs 16:19|Proverbs 16:19}}; see also {{Proverbs 11:2|11:2}}; {{Proverbs 15:33|15:33}}; {{Proverbs 18:12|18:12}}).
Living by deceit is risky. Corrupt people never know when others will discover their treachery or when it will backfire.
This warns against borrowing. Other proverbs advise against guaranteeing others' debts ({{Proverbs 6:1-2|Proverbs 6:1–2}}; {{Proverbs 20:16|20:16}}).
Even a bad ruler wants advisers with a pure heart, meaning they are completely loyal and speak kindly.
This proverb reminds wise people (those with knowledge) that the Lord controls everything.

Among the many proverbs about laziness ({{Proverbs 10:4-6|Proverbs 10:4–6}}, {{Proverbs 10:26|26}}; {{Proverbs 12:11|12:11}}; {{Proverbs 13:4|13:4}}; {{Proverbs 14:4|14:4}}; {{Proverbs 15:19|15:19}}; {{Proverbs 18:9|18:9}}; {{Proverbs 19:15|19:15}}, {{Proverbs 19:24|24}}; {{Proverbs 20:4|20:4}}, {{Proverbs 20:13|13}}; {{Proverbs 21:25|21:25}}; {{Proverbs 26:13|26:13}}), this one is the funniest. Lazy people will invent any wild excuse to avoid working.
An immoral woman uses flattery and seduction to lure a young man into committing a sin.
We learn wisdom; it is not inherited or natural. Discipline is needed to turn foolishness into wisdom.
A person advances through hard work, not by taking advantage of the poor or bribing the wealthy (compare {{Proverbs 22:29|Proverbs 22:29}}).

Like the prologue in the book of Proverbs ({{Proverbs 1:2-7|Proverbs 1:2–7}}) and the introductions to the individual discourses (see {{Proverbs 1:8-9|Proverbs 1:8–9}}; {{Proverbs 2:1-11|2:1–11}}), this section starts by encouraging listening. This wisdom goes beyond practical advice; it aims to inspire trust in the Lord.

This section is attributed to a group known as the wise, but their identity is unknown. There is a mention of thirty sayings ({{Proverbs 22:20|Proverbs 22:20}}). The wisdom sayings that follow can be divided into thirty sections. These sections are similar to an Egyptian work called the *Instruction of Amenemope*, which is also divided into thirty chapters.

*thirty sayings*: Early scribes observed that the Hebrew word for *thirty* was written in an unusual form (*shlshwm*) instead of the usual form (*shlyshym*). All early translations of the Old Testament, such as the Greek Septuagint, Latin Vulgate, and Syriac Peshitta, interpret it as thirty. However, some choose to translate the word as *excellent sayings.*

Saying 1: God protects the weak, including the poor. Those who are wealthy should be generous to the poor ({{Proverbs 11:24-26|Proverbs 11:24–26}}; {{Proverbs 21:13|21:13}}; {{Proverbs 22:9|22:9}}, {{Proverbs 22:16|16}}; {{Proverbs 28:27|28:27}}).
Saying 2: An angry or hot-tempered person cannot control their emotions and shows anger at the wrong times.
This proverb's message is also found in {{Proverbs 6:1-5|Proverbs 6:1–5}}; {{Proverbs 11:15|11:15}}; {{Proverbs 17:18|17:18}}; {{Proverbs 20:16|20:16}}; {{Proverbs 27:13|27:13}}.
Saying 4: In ancient times, stones marked property boundaries. Moving these markers was a serious offense (see also {{Proverbs 23:10|Proverbs 23:10}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:14|Deuteronomy 19:14}}).
Saying 5: People who improve their skills and work hard will get the best jobs and work for the best employers.
Saying 6: Many proverbs advise young men in government jobs. A ruler's rich food might tempt a newcomer to overeat due to lack of self-control. But he will be at risk when full.
Saying 7: Wealth can be a blessing from God ({{Proverbs 3:9-10|Proverbs 3:9–10}}, {{Proverbs 3:15-16|15–16}}; {{Proverbs 10:22|10:22}}), but some things in life matter more.
Saying 9: Fools do not listen to advice (compare {{Proverbs 9:7-12|Proverbs 9:7–12}}; {{Proverbs 10:18|10:18}}), so wise people do not waste their words (see {{Matthew 7:6|Matthew 7:6}}).

- Saying 10: Wise people avoid unfair business practices and illegitimate gains (see {{Proverbs 22:28|Proverbs 22:28}}), knowing that the Lord will judge wrongdoing. 

- *Redeemer*: The New Living Translation is likely correct in capitalizing the word *Redeemer* and identifying it with God, although it might refer to a human redeemer.

Saying 11: Listen carefully: Learning helps you improve (see {{Proverbs 10:17|Proverbs 10:17}}; {{Proverbs 13:1|13:1}}, {{Proverbs 13:10|10}}; {{Proverbs 15:24|15:24}}, {{Proverbs 15:31-32|31–32}}; {{Proverbs 17:10|17:10}}; {{Proverbs 19:24|19:24}}).
Saying 13: A wise parent feels joy when their child is wise (see {{Proverbs 10:1|Proverbs 10:1}}).
Saying 14: Sometimes sinners succeed, but the wise know that fearing the Lord brings true rewards (see {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}).

Saying 15: Discipline is essential for a wise and balanced life. Drinking too much (drunkards, see also {{Proverbs 23:29-35|Proverbs 23:29–35}}), overeating (gluttons, see also {{Proverbs 23:1-3|Proverbs 23:1–3}}), or oversleeping (see also {{Proverbs 10:5|Proverbs 10:5}}; {{Proverbs 19:15|19:15}}) leads to poverty.

Saying 16: This saying encourages seeking the wisdom that both a godly father and mother offer. Unlike other ancient Near East wisdom texts, Proverbs credits wisdom to both parents ({{Proverbs 1:8|Proverbs 1:8}}; {{Proverbs 6:20|6:20}}).

Saying 17: Falling for a promiscuous woman is a trap, not a benefit. Proverbs often warns against sexual relations outside of marriage (see {{Proverbs 5:1-23|Proverbs 5}}; {{Proverbs 6:20-35|6:20–35}}; {{Proverbs 7:1-27|7:1–27}}).
Saying 18: This saying highlights the foolishness of someone who drinks too much alcohol (see {{Proverbs 20:1|Proverbs 20:1}}).
Saying 22: Leaders need to be wise (see {{Proverbs 8:5-6|Proverbs 8:5–6}}).
Saying 23: Fools separate themselves from the community because they do bad things.
Saying 24: A wise person stays calm and strong when stressed (for example, {{Daniel 1:8-16|Daniel 1:8–16}}; {{Daniel 3:1-18|3:1–18}}).
Saying 25: Wise people try to stop injustice and suffering (for example, {{Job 29:12-17|Job 29:12–17}}).
Saying 26: Both honey and wisdom are sweet. Wisdom enriches the soul and creates more future opportunities.
Saying 27: Godly people do not let setbacks keep them down. • Seven times symbolizes "many times."
Saying 28: This saying introduces the teaching of Jesus to love our enemies ({{Matthew 5:43-48|Matthew 5:43–48}}).

- Saying 29: Do not envy the seeming success of the wicked (see {{Proverbs 24:1-2|Proverbs 24:1–2}}), because their success does not last. 

- *extinguished*: Compare {{Proverbs 13:9|Proverbs 13:9}}; {{Proverbs 20:20|20:20}}.
Saying 30: The king is linked to the Lord, showing his power and rule on earth (see {{1 Samuel 12:1-25|1 Samuel 12}}; {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}).
Saying 1: Wise people make fair judgments (see {{Proverbs 6:19|Proverbs 6:19}}; {{Proverbs 12:17|12:17}}; {{Proverbs 19:28|19:28}}; {{Proverbs 24:28-29|24:28–29}}; {{Proverbs 25:18|25:18}}).
This addendum to the thirty sayings of the wise ({{Proverbs 22:17-24:22|Proverbs 22:17–24:22}}) includes five more sayings.
Saying 2: A true friend does not hide problems but honestly shows where you can improve. A wise person appreciates a friend's advice.
Saying 3: A wise person finds a way to earn money before spending it on themselves.

Saying 4: Do not twist the truth, even for revenge (see {{Proverbs 6:19|Proverbs 6:19}}; {{Proverbs 12:17|12:17}}; {{Proverbs 14:25|14:25}}; {{Proverbs 19:28|19:28}}; {{Proverbs 24:23-24|24:23–24}}; {{Proverbs 25:18|25:18}}).

Saying 5: Laziness and a love for sleep can lead to poverty (see {{Proverbs 10:4-5|Proverbs 10:4–5}}, {{Proverbs 10:26|26}}; {{Proverbs 12:11|12:11}}; {{Proverbs 13:4|13:4}}; {{Proverbs 15:19|15:19}}; {{Proverbs 18:9|18:9}}; {{Proverbs 19:15|19:15}}, {{Proverbs 19:24|24}}; {{Proverbs 20:4|20:4}}, {{Proverbs 20:13|13}}).
During King Hezekiah's reign from 728 to 686 BC, advisers gathered these proverbs of Solomon and added them to the collection.

This warning advises young men entering royal service that some things are beyond understanding, like the king's mysterious reasoning (for example, {{2 Samuel 11:14-25|2 Samuel 11:14–25}}; {{2 Samuel 24:3|24:3}}).
Just as silver is useful after removing impurities, the king’s court can do justice when removing wicked people. A small amount of evil can ruin much good ({{Ecclesiastes 10:1|Ecclesiastes 10:1}}).
To meet the king, a wise person will show humility instead of pride (compare {{Matthew 20:20-28|Matthew 20:20–28}}).
Hasty actions often lead to regret.

Timely advice and valid criticism are valuable, beautiful, and rare (see also {{Proverbs 15:23|Proverbs 15:23}}; {{Proverbs 26:7|26:7}}, {{Proverbs 26:9|9}}). We should welcome them (see {{Proverbs 10:17|Proverbs 10:17}}; {{Proverbs 13:1|13:1}}, {{Proverbs 13:10|10}}; {{Proverbs 15:24|15:24}}, {{Proverbs 15:31-32|31–32}}; {{Proverbs 17:10|17:10}}).
Snow would be a welcome relief in Israel’s hot, dry summers (compare {{Proverbs 26:1|Proverbs 26:1}}). Trustworthy messengers refresh their employer by helping them plan for the future.
In Israel, rain is rare. When storm clouds appear but do not bring rain, it is like the disappointment of empty promises. Compare this to Jude’s description of false teachers ({{Jude 12|Jude 1:12}}).

Honey is tasty and healthy in moderation ({{Proverbs 24:13-14|Proverbs 24:13–14}}), but too much can cause vomiting. This idea applies to other life areas. For example, visiting your neighbors is good, but do not visit too often.
Lying can lead to serious consequences (see {{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; {{Proverbs 14:5|14:5}}, {{Proverbs 14:25|25}}).
Surprisingly, showing kindness to an enemy works better than showing anger (see {{Romans 12:20|Romans 12:20}}).
A spring or fountain that provides fresh water gives life. When good people let the wicked control them, what was once life-giving becomes harmful.
Wise people have self-control and are not easily dominated.
It is not right to honor fools.

Curses and blessings can truly impact people (see {{Genesis 27:1-41|Genesis 27:1–41}}; {{Genesis 48:8-9|48:8–9}}, {{Genesis 48:15-20|15–20}}; {{Numbers 6:23-27|Numbers 6:23–27}}), but a curse without cause does not work.
A fool is like a simple animal that needs strong guidance (see {{Proverbs 10:13|Proverbs 10:13}}; {{Proverbs 14:3|14:3}}).
Proverbs often depend on the situation. Deciding whether to respond to foolish arguments depends on the type of fool and the situation.
A fool might know a proverb but not use it correctly. Compare with {{Proverbs 26:9|Proverbs 26:9}}.
A fool using a proverb incorrectly might cause harm. See {{Proverbs 26:7|Proverbs 26:7}}.
A fool or bystander might be lazy (see {{Proverbs 10:4-6|Proverbs 10:4–6}}) or incompetent (see {{Proverbs 26:6-7|26:6–7}}). Employers should be cautious!
Even when foolish actions cause serious problems, a fool continues to act foolishly ({{Proverbs 17:10|Proverbs 17:10}}; see also {{2 Peter 2:22|2 Peter 2:22}}).
Fools have hope because they might realize their mistakes and ask for help. However, those who believe they are wise will stay ignorant.
This proverb is the same as {{Proverbs 19:24|Proverbs 19:24}}.
Wise people stay out of other people's arguments (compare {{Proverbs 26:21|Proverbs 26:21}}).

Lies are very dangerous because they make people act on false information. Liars cannot later claim they were only joking (see {{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; {{Proverbs 14:5|14:5}}, {{Proverbs 14:25|25}}; {{Proverbs 25:18|25:18}}).
A gossip and a quarrelsome person both add fuel to the fire of trouble and conflict.
People sometimes hide bad intentions with flattery. Eventually, the true hatred of those who speak smoothly will be revealed.
People often face the negative outcomes they plan for others (see {{Proverbs 1:17-19|Proverbs 1:17–19}}).

We should plan ({{Proverbs 24:27|Proverbs 24:27}}), but our plans succeed only if God wills it ({{Proverbs 16:1|Proverbs 16:1}}, {{Proverbs 16:3|3}}, {{Proverbs 16:33|33}}; {{James 4:13-16|James 4:13–16}}). Only foolish people think they control the future.
The Hebrew word for praise comes from the same root as "brag" in {{Proverbs 27:1|Proverbs 27:1}}. Bragging, or self-praise, is unwise.
Fools create strong resentment with their foolish words and actions.
Anger can be dangerous, but a gentle answer can calm it ({{Proverbs 15:1|Proverbs 15:1}}). Jealousy is more difficult to resolve ({{Proverbs 6:34-35|Proverbs 6:34–35}}).
A rebuke can improve life by correcting harmful behavior ({{Proverbs 13:1|Proverbs 13:1}}; {{Proverbs 14:6|14:6}}). Hidden, unexpressed love has no value.
Wounds from a friend come from a caring correction ({{Proverbs 27:5|Proverbs 27:5}}). They are better than flattery (*kisses*) from an enemy who wants to harm, not help.
Even the best teaching (*honey*) will be ignored if given at the wrong time. The key to real learning is the student's willingness to learn.
A person who leaves his family and home is more likely to find trouble than what he was looking for (for example, {{Luke 15:11-16|Luke 15:11–16}}).
Heartfelt advice from a close friend is very encouraging (see also {{Proverbs 27:6|Proverbs 27:6}}).
During a crisis, you might need help right away. It is important to have friends nearby and neighbors who can assist.
People often judge parents based on how their children behave in public.
It is important to speak appropriately for the situation (compare {{Proverbs 15:23|Proverbs 15:23}}).
*iron sharpens iron*: Wisdom comes from interacting, often critically, with a good friend (see {{Proverbs 27:6|Proverbs 27:6}}, {{Proverbs 27:9|9}}).

An employer values loyal workers who safeguard the employer’s interests. Smart employers offer incentives for loyalty, like letting workers enjoy the benefits of their labor (see {{Deuteronomy 25:4|Deuteronomy 25:4}}; {{1 Corinthians 9:7-10|1 Corinthians 9:7–10}}; {{1 Timothy 5:17-18|1 Timothy 5:17–18}}).

- *Sheol and Abaddon*: See study note on Proverbs 15:11. 

- People never find true satisfaction in money, power, or pleasure.
A person who stays humble when praised shows a pure character (see {{Proverbs 17:3|Proverbs 17:3}}).
A fool's character is full of foolishness.
Agricultural property can provide food and clothing for generations. These resources need constant work and care, or they will vanish like riches.
The wicked face God's curse for breaking his covenant (see {{Leviticus 26:14-17|Leviticus 26:14–17}}, {{Leviticus 26:36-37|36–37}}).
Wise leaders rule with justice and effectiveness ({{Proverbs 8:15-16|Proverbs 8:15–16}}).
Without laws, chaos happens and bad people thrive.
Bad people try to benefit by breaking the law. Justice makes sure they are punished, while good people receive rewards.
Virtue is more valuable than material wealth. This idea is repeated with a slightly different conclusion in {{Proverbs 19:1|Proverbs 19:1}}.
*his father*: This saying applies to both fathers and mothers.

The law forbade charging interest on loans to needy Israelites ({{Exodus 22:25|Exodus 22:25}}; {{Leviticus 25:36|Leviticus 25:36}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:19|Deuteronomy 23:19}}). The rich were told to lend generously to the poor ({{Proverbs 3:27-28|Proverbs 3:27–28}}; {{Proverbs 11:24|11:24}}; {{Proverbs 28:27|28:27}}; {{Proverbs 29:7|29:7}}, {{Proverbs 29:14|14}}).
A person who ignores the law does not respect the Lord ({{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}), the one who gives the law. That person's prayers are insincere, so why should God listen?
Wise people admit their mistakes and wrongdoings and seek to correct them (see {{Psalm 32:1-5|Psalm 32:1–5}}).
An unjust ruler will not help the poor. Like a roaring lion or an attacking bear, he ruins their lives.

- *burdened by bloodguilt*: See {{1 Samuel 25:31|1 Samuel 25:31}}; {{Romans 2:15|Romans 2:15}}; {{Romans 13:5|13:5}}; compare {{Hebrews 10:22|Hebrews 10:22}}.

- *let no one support him*: Murder is so serious that a fine cannot replace the death penalty (see {{Numbers 35:32|Numbers 35:32}}).
This proverb appears again with a different ending in {{Proverbs 12:11|Proverbs 12:11}}.

*abound with blessings*: You must earn wealth ethically, or it will cause harm and not last (see {{Proverbs 13:11|Proverbs 13:11}}, compare {{Proverbs 10:2|10:2}}; {{Proverbs 11:18|11:18}}; {{Proverbs 13:22|13:22}}; {{Proverbs 21:6|21:6}}).
Giving a wrong verdict because of a bribe is wrong ({{Proverbs 17:23|Proverbs 17:23}}; {{Proverbs 22:16|22:16}}).

Wise people want honest feedback about their mistakes so they can improve ({{Proverbs 10:17|Proverbs 10:17}}; {{Proverbs 13:1|13:1}}, {{Proverbs 13:10|10}}; {{Proverbs 15:24|15:24}}, {{Proverbs 15:31-32|31–32}}).
Children who take advantage of their parents are wrong (see {{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}).
Greedy people fight to control situations to gain wealth. Trusting the Lord helps wise people stay calm and, surprisingly, find prosperity.
Wise people listen to others' advice, while those who only trust themselves act foolishly.
*When the wicked come to power*: See also {{Proverbs 28:12|Proverbs 28:12}}.

- A man's wisdom influences his parents ({{Proverbs 10:1|Proverbs 10:1}}; {{Proverbs 15:20|15:20}}; {{Proverbs 17:21|17:21}}). 

- Spending money on prostitutes quickly wastes a man's wealth.

A fair king protects the rights of others. A ruler who takes bribes uses his position for personal benefit (see also {{Proverbs 17:23|Proverbs 17:23}}; {{Proverbs 22:16|22:16}}; {{Proverbs 28:21|28:21}}).
Flattery is often a trick to exploit someone ({{Proverbs 7:21-22|Proverbs 7:21–22}}; {{Proverbs 26:23|26:23}}).
Wise people control their emotions and stay calm, even when stressed.

The oppressor should treat the poor more kindly because God created both of them (see also {{Proverbs 3:27|Proverbs 3:27}}; {{Proverbs 11:24|11:24}}; {{Proverbs 28:27|28:27}}; {{Proverbs 29:7|29:7}}).
Wisdom is not natural; it must be learned.
Wise people follow God's law, which shows His will.
Sometimes, you may need to add clear consequences to instructions for discipline.
*fear of man is a snare*: See {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}; {{Luke 12:4-5|Luke 12:4–5}}.

- This superscription likely refers to all of {{Proverbs 30:1-33|Proverbs 30}}. 

- *Agur son of Jakeh*: Besides this mention, Agur and Jakeh are not known. If “from Massa” is correct, as some translations use, then Agur was not an Israelite (the tribe of Massa is known from Assyrian texts).
Agur admits he does not know everything (compare {{Psalm 73:22|Psalm 73:22}}, where the psalmist calls himself *senseless*). The first step toward wisdom is admitting our ignorance.
Unlike Agur's lack of knowledge and power, God's strength and wisdom are evident (compare {{Psalm 18:30|Psalm 18:30}}). This is encouraging to Agur, as he knows God protects everyone who seeks Him.

Agur asks God for two things: 

- Help to avoid lying (compare {{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; {{Proverbs 14:5|14:5}}, {{Proverbs 14:25|25}}; {{Proverbs 25:18|25:18}}; {{Proverbs 26:18-19|26:18–19}})

- To not have too much or too little

Being rich ({{Proverbs 3:9-10|Proverbs 3:9–10}}, {{Proverbs 3:15-16|15–16}}; {{Proverbs 10:15|10:15}}, {{Proverbs 10:22|22}}) or poor ({{Proverbs 3:27|3:27}}; {{Proverbs 11:24|11:24}}; {{Proverbs 28:27|28:27}}; {{Proverbs 29:7|29:7}}, {{Proverbs 29:14|14}}) is not sinful, but Agur wisely wants to avoid the problems of both.

These verses describe traits that wise people dislike. Fools: 

- Disrespect their parents ({{Proverbs 10:1|Proverbs 10:1}}; {{Proverbs 20:20|20:20}}; {{Exodus 20:12|Exodus 20:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:16|Deuteronomy 5:16}})

- Deceive themselves ({{Proverbs 8:7|Proverbs 8:7}})

- Think they are clean when they are not ({{Proverbs 20:9|Proverbs 20:9}})

- Are proud ({{Proverbs 6:17-18|Proverbs 6:17–18}}; {{Proverbs 11:2|11:2}}; {{Proverbs 13:10|13:10}}; {{Proverbs 15:33|15:33}}; {{Proverbs 16:18|16:18}}; {{Proverbs 18:12|18:12}}; {{Proverbs 19:20|19:20}}; {{Proverbs 29:23|29:23}})

- Hurt others with their words (teeth like swords, see {{Proverbs 25:18|Proverbs 25:18}})

- Harm the poor ({{Proverbs 3:27|Proverbs 3:27}}; {{Proverbs 11:24|11:24}}; {{Proverbs 28:27|28:27}}; {{Proverbs 29:7|29:7}}, {{Proverbs 29:14|14}})

- The number parallelism (*three...four*) is a method to list poetic examples. This list shows powers that are never satisfied and often dangerous. See also {{Proverbs 30:18-19|Proverbs 30:18–19}}, {{Proverbs 30:21-23|21–23}}, {{Proverbs 30:29-31|29–31}}.

- The grave, representing death, never seems to have enough—people keep dying ({{Proverbs 27:20|Proverbs 27:20}}).

- *barren womb*: Women unable to have children often long for them, like Sarah before Isaac, Rebekah before Esau and Jacob, and Hannah before Samuel. 

- The thirsty desert and a fire consume everything in their path.

People who are unkind to their parents may face a harsh fate (see {{Proverbs 10:1|Proverbs 10:1}}; {{Proverbs 19:26|19:26}}; {{Proverbs 28:24|28:24}}; {{Proverbs 29:3|29:3}}; {{Proverbs 30:11|30:11}}).
The writer is amazed at how one thing affects another.
The writer is shocked by sex outside of marriage.

- This proverb lists four things that make the earth tremble because they disrupt the natural order. 

- *who is filled with food*: In the ancient Near East, as in many non-industrialized parts of the world today, having enough food was a sign of prosperity.
Here is another example of number parallelism: small, seemingly insignificant animals can be surprisingly powerful and resourceful.
